insights.insight: Ad tech charges $5–$150 CPA for probabilistic attribution that infers purchase intent. This protocol settles at ~$0.10 per cryptographically verified receipt — a 50–200x cost delta that isn't a pricing negotiation, it's a structural difference in what you're buying.

Cookies are gone, device fingerprinting is degrading, and data broker utility is shrinking under GDPR and state privacy laws — the probabilistic targeting stack is being dismantled from multiple directions simultaneously, with no industry-wide replacement in production.

insights.topic: Receipt as conversion proof, not proxy
insights.insight: A verified receipt eliminates the attribution problem entirely: no lookback window, no modeled conversion, no pixel dependency. The purchase event is the signal, not an inference about it.

Amazon knows Amazon purchases. Walmart knows Walmart purchases. Neither has visibility into cross-retailer behavior. Any system that aggregates verified purchase signals across ecosystems without identity attachment creates an information asymmetry that every brand competing across channels needs.

insights.topic: Geographic diffusion pattern as adoption signal
insights.insight: Ten new metros entered in a single cycle — including non-metro California, Arkansas, and Indiana simultaneously — following a burst-silence-burst pattern consistent with word-of-mouth propagation, not paid acquisition. This is organic geographic spread with no common regional logic, which is a harder signal to manufacture and a more durable one.

insights.topic: Unknown merchant category as data quality flag
insights.insight: 11% of receipts resist merchant classification and carry a $290 average basket — 5.5x the grocery average — likely high-ticket or B2B transactions. Any brand using this data for category analysis needs to account for this gap; entropy and cross-domain metrics built on unresolved merchants are interpreted, not verified.
